q: Who are the main gods in Hindu mythology?
Tell me about the Hindu Trimurti
Who are Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva?
What is the Hindu pantheon?
Describe the major Hindu deities
What are the roles of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva?
a: Hindu mythology features a vast pantheon, with the supreme trinity (Trimurti) representing the three fundamental cosmic functions. Brahma is the creator god, born from a lotus from Vishnu's navel, who creates the universe and all beings; he has four faces representing the four Vedas and is typically depicted holding a water pot, a spoon, prayer beads, and the Vedas. Vishnu is the preserver god who maintains cosmic order (dharma) and has incarnated on earth in ten major avatars (Dashavatara), including Rama (hero of the Ramayana), Krishna (divine statesman from the Mahabharata), and Buddha. Shiva is the destroyer and transformer god, whose cosmic dance (Nataraja) represents the cycle of creation, preservation, and destruction; he is often depicted with a third eye, a trident, a crescent moon on his head, and the Ganges River flowing through his matted hair. The goddess Devi (in her forms as Saraswati, Lakshmi, and Parvati/Durga/Kali) is venerated as the supreme divine feminine power (Shakti).

q: What are the main elements of Chinese mythology?
Tell me about Chinese dragons
Who is the Jade Emperor in Chinese mythology?
Describe Chinese mythological creatures
What are the Four Symbols in Chinese mythology?
Tell me about Chinese gods and legends
a: Chinese mythology is a rich tapestry of ancient legends, philosophical concepts, and folk religion spanning thousands of years. Chinese dragons (Lóng) are benevolent, wise creatures associated with water, rainfall, and imperial power — unlike the fire-breathing dragons of Western myth, they are serpentine beings with five claws (for imperial dragons) who control rivers, seas, and weather, and symbolize strength, good fortune, and yang energy. The Jade Emperor (Yù Huáng) is the supreme ruler of Heaven and the celestial bureaucracy in Taoist mythology, governing a vast heavenly court with a complex hierarchy of gods, immortals, and officials. The Four Symbols (Sì Xiàng) are four mythological creatures representing the cardinal directions: the Azure Dragon of the East, the Vermilion Bird of the South, the White Tiger of the West, and the Black Tortoise of the North. The Eight Immortals (Bā Xiān) are legendary Taoist figures who achieved immortality, each possessing a magical object and representing different walks of life. The myth of Pangu describes a cosmic giant who emerged from a cosmic egg, separated heaven and earth, and whose body became the mountains, rivers, and stars after his death.

q: What are the main myths of Japanese mythology?
Tell me about Amaterasu, the sun goddess
Who is Susanoo in Japanese myth?
Describe Japanese Shinto mythology
What is the story of Izanagi and Izanami?
Who are the major Japanese gods?
a: Japanese mythology is deeply rooted in Shinto, the indigenous faith of Japan, and centers on the kami (spirits or gods) who inhabit all aspects of nature. Amaterasu Ōmikami (the Great August Sun Goddess) is the chief deity of the Shinto pantheon and the mythical ancestor of the Japanese imperial family. According to myth, she retreated into a cave after a quarrel with her brother Susanoo, plunging the world into darkness, and was only lured out by the other gods' festivities, particularly the lewd dance of the goddess Ame-no-Uzume. Susanoo, the storm god, was Amaterasu's wild and unpredictable brother who was banished from heaven for his destructive behavior; he later redeemed himself by slaying the eight-headed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi and rescuing the goddess Kushinada-hime. The creation myth begins with Izanagi and Izanami, the divine couple who stirred the primordial ocean with a jeweled spear to create the first land, and gave birth to the many islands of Japan and the kami — though Izanami died giving birth to the fire god and descended to Yomi (the underworld), from which Izanagi narrowly escaped.

q: What is Mesopotamian mythology?
Who was Gilgamesh?
What is the Epic of Gilgamesh?
Tell me about the Enuma Elish creation myth
What are the main Mesopotamian gods?
Describe Sumerian and Babylonian mythology
a: Mesopotamian mythology, originating from Sumer, Akkad, Babylonia, and Assyria, is among the oldest recorded mythologies in human history. The Epic of Gilgamesh is the oldest known work of literature, dating from around 2100 BCE, telling the story of Gilgamesh, the semi-divine king of Uruk, and his journey with the wild man Enkidu to slay the demon Humbaba and defeat the Bull of Heaven. After Enkidu's death, Gilgamesh embarks on a quest for immortality, ultimately learning that true meaning lies in living a good life rather than escaping death. The Enuma Elish is the Babylonian creation epic in which the god Marduk (or in earlier versions, the Assyrian god Ashur) defeats the chaotic primordial sea goddess Tiamat, splits her body into two halves to form heaven and earth, and creates humanity from the blood of her consort Kingu. Major Mesopotamian deities include Anu (god of the sky and supreme ruler), Enlil (god of wind and storms), Enki/Ea (god of wisdom, water, and creation who warned humanity of the flood), Ishtar/Inanna (goddess of love, beauty, and war who descended to the underworld), and Shamash/Utu (sun god of justice).

q: What is Celtic mythology?
Tell me about Celtic gods and legends
Who were the Tuatha Dé Danann?
Describe Celtic mythology and its deities
What are the main myths of the Celts?
Who are the most important Celtic gods?
a: Celtic mythology encompasses the pagan beliefs of the ancient Celtic peoples across Ireland, Britain, Gaul, and other parts of Europe, preserved largely through medieval Irish and Welsh manuscripts after Christianization. The Tuatha Dé Danann (Tribe of the Goddess Danu) are the supernatural race of gods and heroes in Irish mythology who arrived in Ireland on a cloud and later retreated into the hills and mounds (sídhe) to become the fairy folk after being defeated by the Milesians (the human ancestors of the Irish). Major Celtic deities include Dagda (the 'Good God,' a father figure with a magical club and cauldron of abundance), Lugh (the god of skill, crafts, and warfare, also known as Lugh of the Long Arm), Brigid (goddess of poetry, healing, and smithcraft, later Christianized as Saint Brigid), Morrigan (the phantom queen goddess of war, fate, and death who often appeared as a crow), Cernunnos (the horned god of nature, animals, and fertility depicted on the Gundestrup Cauldron), and Epona (the horse goddess worshipped across the Celtic world by Romans as well). The most famous Celtic myth cycles include the Ulster Cycle (featuring the demigod hero Cú Chulainn, who defended Ulster single-handedly against the armies of Connacht) and the Mythological Cycle (chronicling the Tuatha Dé Danann and their battles). Celtic mythology also introduced enduring legends such as King Arthur, the Holy Grail, and the hero Finn McCool with his band of warriors the Fianna.

q: What are the similarities between world mythologies?
How do different mythologies compare?
What common themes appear across world mythologies?
Tell me about shared motifs in mythology
What archetypes appear across different mythological traditions?
a: Despite emerging from vastly different cultures and time periods, world mythologies share remarkable structural similarities and recurring archetypes. The comparative mythologist Joseph Campbell identified the 'monomyth' or Hero's Journey—a universal pattern where a hero leaves their ordinary world, ventures into a supernatural realm, faces trials, achieves a decisive victory, and returns transformed—that appears in stories from Gilgamesh to the Buddha to Jesus. Most pantheons include a sky father god (Zeus, Odin, Ra, Tianzhu, Indra), an earth mother goddess (Gaia, Jord, Nut, Prithvi), a trickster figure (Loki, Hermes, Coyote, Eshu, Anansi), and a dying-and-rising god (Osiris, Baldr, Dionysus, Tammuz). Creation myths often begin with a primordial chaos or cosmic egg (Greek Chaos, Chinese Pangu, Hindu Hiranyagarbha, Egyptian Benben), and flood myths appear in nearly every tradition (Noah in the Bible, Utnapishtim in Gilgamesh, Deucalion in Greek myth, Manu in Hindu tradition). These commonalities suggest that mythology reflects universal human psychological patterns, shared existential questions, and the need to explain natural phenomena through narrative.
